**Atlas does not meet your Korean data requirement, so it should not be chosen for LUMEN as it stands.** It can host data only in Frankfurt (EU) and Oregon (US).

**Price:** The rate is USD 0.42 per 1,000 queries, and there is a minimum commitment of USD 18,000 per year. At 40 million queries, usage comes to USD 16,800. That is below the minimum, so you would pay **USD 18,000 per year**, which is within your USD 25,000 ceiling. Usage could rise to about 59.5 million queries before the bill went above the USD 18,000 minimum, and to about 59.5 million × (25,000 ÷ 18,000) ≈ 59.5 million before it neared the ceiling. More precisely, the ceiling is reached at about 59.5 million queries, so you have roughly 49% headroom over your estimate.

**SLA:** Atlas promises 99.95% monthly uptime. Service credits are 10% for each 0.1% below that. The file gives no cap on credits, no claim process and no definition of what counts as downtime.

**Data residency:** Only the EU (Frankfurt) and the US (Oregon) are offered. There is no Korean region, so the requirement that Korean customer data stays in Korea is not met.

I read all 40 sections. Apart from one line each for price, SLA and residency, the file is repetitive filler with no other terms, such as contract length, overage rules or exceptions to residency. If Atlas is still a candidate, ask them in writing whether a Korean region or an in-country option exists. That is the question for Jae-won Park to have answered before a decision.

**Borealis meets your Korean data requirement on paper. It costs about USD 14,000 per year before data-transfer charges and has a lower uptime promise than Atlas.**

**Price:** The rate is USD 0.35 per 1,000 queries, with no minimum commitment. At 40 million queries that is **USD 14,000 per year**. Data leaving the service (egress) is billed separately at USD 0.09 per GB. That leaves USD 11,000 of room under your USD 25,000 ceiling, which covers about 122 TB of egress. The file does not say how much egress LUMEN would use, so that cost is unknown.

**SLA:** 99.9% monthly uptime. The file does not mention service credits or any other remedy if Borealis falls short. That is weaker than Atlas, which promised 99.95% with credits.

**Data residency:** Seoul (ap-northeast-2), Tokyo and Singapore. Seoul satisfies your requirement. The file does not say whether you can restrict data to Seoul only, or whether Tokyo and Singapore are used for backups or processing. Ask Borealis to confirm in writing before Jae-won Park decides.

**Certification:** ISMS-P certified since March 2025. The file does not give the certificate scope or the expiry date.

**Cirrus fits your budget and keeps data in Seoul, with the strongest uptime promise of the three vendors so far.** Its Seoul hosting runs through a partner, which needs a check.

**Price:** The rate is USD 0.50 per 1,000 queries. At 40 million queries that is **USD 20,000 per year** on a standard term. **SLA:** 99.99% monthly uptime, with a 15-minute response time for top-priority (P1) incidents. The file gives no service credits or other remedy if Cirrus misses the uptime figure.

The file mentions no security certification, so I can't say whether Cirrus holds ISMS-P, which Borealis does.
